**Defense in depth** is the practice of protecting an important guarantee with several independent layers,
so that when one layer fails, another still catches the problem.
The name comes from security engineering,
where a system is protected by multiple countermeasures rather than a single wall.
@reason2000human described the same idea for accidents in complex systems as the "Swiss cheese" model:
each defense has holes, like a slice of Swiss cheese,
and an accident happens only when the holes in every layer line up.
Adding a layer does not remove the holes in the others;
it makes it less likely that a problem passes through all of them.

In research software, the guarantees worth layering include:

- that results can be reproduced from the code and data;
- that code merged to the main branch passes its tests;
- that private data never reaches a public repository.

Each of these can be guarded by several layers:

- **Prevention** before the mistake, such as a type or argument check, or a pre-commit hook.
- **Detection** soon after it, such as a test or a lint check that runs on every push.
- **Review**, in which a person or a separate tool reads the change.
- **Recovery** after it, such as version control, which lets you revert a bad change.

### Make the layers independent

Layers protect only if they do not fail for the same reason.
Two checks that run the same script, read the same configuration,
or depend on the same service fail together,
and count as one layer.
Prefer layers that differ in mechanism (a test, a linter, a reviewer),
in timing (before a commit, in CI, at review),
and in who or what operates them.

### Test each layer on its own

A layer that fails silently is worse than no layer,
because it makes the guarantee look protected when it is not.
Test each layer separately from the others:
give it an input it must catch, and confirm that it does.
For example, to test a linter in CI,
push a branch with a deliberate violation and confirm that the check fails.
Do this when the check is first added and again whenever it changes,
since a configuration error often turns a check into one that always passes.

A check that reports success should also show that it ran.
A check that finds nothing because it inspected nothing
(an empty file list, a wrong path, a skipped step)
looks the same as a check that found nothing wrong.
Have each layer fail, or say so loudly, when it has nothing to check,
in keeping with the principle of failing fast
(see [Assertions and Input Validation](coding-style.qmd#sec-assertions-input-validation)).

### Layers have a cost

Each layer costs time to build, maintain and wait for,
and several layers guarding a trivial guarantee are over-engineered
(see [KISS](#sec-kiss)).
Reserve defense in depth for guarantees whose failure is costly or hard to notice,
such as a wrong result in a published analysis.
